overview:
Within the Śvetāmbara Mūrtipūjaka tradition, “Murtipujaka lists” most commonly refers to the catalogues of monastic lineages and orders (gaccha) that structure the image‑worshipping community. These lists function as historical, ritual, and identity markers: they record which gacchas existed, how they traced their spiritual descent, and how they differentiated themselves in matters of practice while remaining doctrinally Śvetāmbara. In community memory and in modern scholarship, the most famous of these is the set of “84 gacchas” associated with the Mūrtipūjaka Śvetāmbara Jains.

The term gaccha (from Sanskrit/Prakrit roots meaning “those who go/travel together”) designates a monastic order together with its lay following. In early Śvetāmbara Mūrtipūjaka history, tradition reports that the monk Vajrasensuri divided the community into four kulas (Chandra, Nirvṛti, Vidyādhara, and Nāgendra) during a time of drought, and that later—roughly between the 7th–8th and 11th–13th centuries CE—gacchas replaced these kulas as the primary organizational units. Over time, many gacchas arose, flourished, merged, or disappeared, and the remembered total of “84” became a symbolic way of speaking about the diversity of Mūrtipūjaka orders rather than a fixed, universally agreed list.

Published Murtipujaka lists of the 84 gacchas, whether in colonial‑era compilations or later community histories, are notably discordant. Different manuscripts, oral traditions, and regional memories preserve overlapping but non‑identical sequences of names. Nonetheless, certain gacchas recur across most lists: Upakeśa (often singled out as the oldest and uniquely tracing its lineage to Pārśvanātha), Kharatara, Tapā, Āchal (Achal), Paichand/Parśvachandra, and others. These lists typically mix orders that survived into the modern period with those that are now only remembered by name, and they sometimes include lay‑community labels (such as Oswāl) that later became primarily caste or regional identifiers.

For Mūrtipūjaka Jains, such lists are not merely historical curiosities. They are embedded in narrative literature, temple inscriptions, and monastic genealogies, and they help locate particular communities—such as Kharatara Gaccha or Tapā Gaccha—within the broader Śvetāmbara landscape. In some cases, the lists are invoked to assert antiquity or orthodoxy: a gaccha may be praised as one of the “original” 84, or as uniquely preserving a lineage from a specific Tīrthaṅkara. In other cases, they serve to remember reform movements, such as the Achal Gaccha’s emphasis on strict adherence to vidhi (prescribed monastic discipline) within the Mūrtipūjaka framework.

From a technical and historical perspective, scholars treat Murtipujaka lists cautiously. Because the lists are late, often regionally shaped, and sometimes reconstructed from oral testimony, they cannot be read as straightforward evidence for early Jain history. Instead, they are valuable as windows into how Mūrtipūjaka communities in different periods imagined their own past, organized their present, and negotiated relations with other Śvetāmbara sects (Sthānakavāsī, Terāpanthī) and with Digambara gacchas. The lists also highlight an important feature of Jain tradition: doctrinal continuity can coexist with significant diversity in ritual calendars, temple practices, and monastic discipline, all of which are reflected in the names and reputations of individual gacchas.

Modern Mūrtipūjaka practice continues to be shaped by a smaller number of active gacchas, especially Tapā Gaccha and Kharatara Gaccha, whose monastic leaders, institutions, and scriptural curricula are central to contemporary Śvetāmbara life. In this context, historical Murtipujaka lists are often referenced in community education, sermons, and scholarship to situate these living orders within a long lineage of image‑worshipping Śvetāmbara Jainism. At the same time, responsible study of these lists requires attention to the difference between primary canonical texts, later narrative and genealogical works, and modern reconstructions, and it benefits from consultation with qualified scholars and monastic authorities when questions of lineage, authority, or sectarian affiliation arise.

primary_sources.title: Kalpa Sūtra
primary_sources.author: Traditionally attributed to Bhadrabāhu; redacted within the Śvetāmbara canon
primary_sources.translation: The Kalpa Sūtra is a Śvetāmbara canonical text recounting the lives of Tīrthaṅkaras, monastic regulations, and ritual prescriptions, widely copied, worshipped, and recited in Mūrtipūjaka communities, especially during Paryuṣaṇa.
primary_sources.notes: Although the Kalpa Sūtra does not itself present lists of Mūrtipūjaka gacchas, it is central to the ritual and scholastic life of major Mūrtipūjaka orders such as Tapā Gaccha and Kharatara Gaccha. Manuscript traditions, colophons, and community histories surrounding the Kalpa Sūtra are key tier‑A and tier‑C sources for understanding how these gacchas situate themselves within Śvetāmbara Mūrtipūjaka Jainism and how they frame their own lineages and reforms.

primary_sources.title: Gaccha‑sthapana and lineage narratives in Śvetāmbara Jain tradition
primary_sources.author: Anonymous and various monastic authors in Prakrit and Sanskrit
primary_sources.translation: These narrative and genealogical texts recount the founding of specific gacchas, the lives of their ācāryas, and the transmission of monastic discipline and ritual practice across generations.
primary_sources.notes: Accounts of Vajrasensuri’s division of the community into four kulas, and later stories of the establishment of gacchas such as Upakeśa, Kharatara, Tapā, and Achal, are preserved in a mixture of inscriptions, prabandha‑style narratives, and monastic chronicles. They form the primary traditional basis for many of the names that appear in Murtipujaka lists of the 84 gacchas. Because these materials vary in date, language, and reliability, careful comparison and source criticism are necessary when using them to reconstruct historical developments.

misconceptions.myth: The “84 Murtipujaka gacchas” are a single, fixed list that all Śvetāmbara Jains agree upon and that directly reflects the earliest history of the tradition.
misconceptions.reality: Existing lists of the 84 gacchas are discordant, shaped by regional memory and later reconstruction, and they mix historically attested orders with names known only from tradition. They are valuable for understanding how Mūrtipūjaka communities imagine and narrate their past, but they cannot be treated as a simple, uniform record of early Jain history.

misconceptions.myth: Each gaccha in the Murtipujaka lists represents a separate doctrinal sect with its own scriptures and theology.
misconceptions.reality: Mūrtipūjaka gacchas share Śvetāmbara doctrine and canonical authority; their differences lie primarily in matters of practice—ritual calendars, disciplinary strictness, and lineage customs—rather than in separate theologies or canons. The lists therefore map internal diversity of practice within a common doctrinal framework, not competing religions.

misconceptions.myth: Modern Śvetāmbara Mūrtipūjaka life is still organized around all 84 gacchas listed in traditional catalogues.
misconceptions.reality: Only a small number of gacchas, such as Tapā Gaccha and Kharatara Gaccha, remain prominent in contemporary Mūrtipūjaka Jainism. Many names in the traditional lists refer to orders that have merged, declined, or survive only in memory. Today, historical Murtipujaka lists are primarily educational and historiographical tools rather than direct administrative maps of the living community.
